pages.x: In March 2011, inspired by the revolts in Tunisia and Egypt, teenage boys in the southern town of Daraa sprayed slogans against the government on a school wall. They were arrested and tortured. Protests for their release spread across Syria, and the security forces answered with live fire.

Bashar al-Assad, an eye doctor trained in London, had inherited Syria in 2000 from his father, Hafez, who had ruled it for 29 years. He had promised reform, but he called the protests a foreign plot and crushed them. Soldiers who refused to shoot deserted, and formed the Free Syrian Army.

By 2012 the war had reached Aleppo, Syria's largest city, which was split in two for four years. Government helicopters dropped barrel bombs, oil drums packed with explosives, on rebel-held districts. In December 2016, after a siege backed by Russian air power, the government took the whole city, much of it in ruins.

In August 2013 rockets filled with sarin, a nerve gas, hit Ghouta, rebel-held suburbs of Damascus, and killed hundreds of people, many of them children, as they slept. Most governments and investigators blamed Assad's forces, who denied it. Syria agreed to give up its chemical weapons, but gas attacks went on.
pages.of: killed by nerve gas in one night

pages.x: In 2014 the Islamic State, an extremist group grown out of al-Qaeda in Iraq, seized a third of Syria and much of Iraq, and its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, declared a caliphate. From its capital, Raqqa, it ruled by terror, filming beheadings for the internet. Kurdish-led forces backed by American planes destroyed it by 2019.

In 2015 Russia sent its air force to save Assad, while Iran and Hezbollah from Lebanon sent fighters. Turkey backed rebels in the north, and the United States backed the Kurds. Syria became a battleground for half the world's powers, and by 2020 Assad held most of the country again, its cities in ruins.

Half of all Syrians were driven from their homes. About six million fled abroad, most to Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and in 2015 hundreds of thousands made for Europe, many in flimsy boats. The photograph of a drowned three-year-old boy, Alan Kurdi, on a Turkish beach moved the world.

In late November 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, under Ahmed al-Sharaa, burst out of their stronghold in Idlib. City after city fell almost without a fight, and on 8 December they entered Damascus. Assad fled to Moscow. Crowds poured into his prisons, freeing thousands, and searched for the missing.

Thirteen years of war killed over half a million people and scattered half of Syria's people across the world. The fall of the Assad family, after more than fifty years in power, brought joy and hope, but also fears of new violence, and the long work of rebuilding a ruined country.
